abstract: Synthetic data is increasingly important for machine learning in domains where real-world data is scarce, sensitive, imbalanced, or costly to obtain. By generating realistic and controllable datasets, it enables robust training, improves performance on rare cases, and supports privacypreserving development. In this work, we investigate synthetic data generation methods across space operations use cases spanning multiple modalities: documentation (text), telemetry (time series), and optical telescope imagery. We report results and lessons learned from applying these methods in operationally relevant scenarios.

blocks.html: The increasing adoption of AI in space operations raises challenges related to data availability, quality, and representativeness. Operational datasets are often incomplete, imbalanced, sensitive, or difficult to share, limiting the development and evaluation of downstream machine learning systems. Synthetic data offers a potential solution by enabling controlled data generation tailored to specific tasks and constraints.

The SYNDAQ (Synthetic Data Generation and Qualification) project assesses the benefits and limitations of synthetic data for downstream tasks typical of space operations. The project focuses on four representative use cases: (1) Synthetic RAG evaluation benchmark generation from documentation, where a “silver dataset” is automatically constructed to enable systematic evaluation of retrieval-augmented generation systems; (2) Telemetry gap filling, where synthetic methods reconstruct missing segments in time series data; (3) Telemetry generation, where new telemetry datasets are generated to augment or re-ensemble existing ones; (4) Synthetic FITS image generation matching STREET telescope characteristics for space debris classification, where optical images with realistic artifacts are simulated.

blocks.title: Synthetic RAG Evaluation Benchmark Generation from Documents

blocks.html: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is increasingly used to answer questions grounded in proprietary technical documents such as procedures, technical reports, and user manuals. Yet most teams start a RAG project without an evaluation benchmark that reflects their mission data. They often hand-craft small test sets manually, which is time-consuming. The challenge of mission-specific evaluation arises every sprint: teams need to measure the effect of changes to their AI system (new prompts, new embedding models, or new LLMs). This evaluation dataset is also needed to measure progress quantitatively as the project matures.

The syndaqa python library developped in this project enable AI teams to generate synthetic evaluation data directly from documents. It helps the early development of RAG system, when domain expertise is scarce, and the AI team needs to set up their RAG MVP quickly.

The software uses large language models (LLMs) to synthetically generate mission-specific evaluation datasets, whereas traditional methods rely on human annotation. The goal is not to create a perfect, "golden" benchmark instantly. Instead, the synthetic data generators target a "silver" dataset: a set of high-value question–answer–source triplets that is sufficient to support systematic, repeatable evaluations, even if imperfect. The generated dataset is grounded in available documents, and a highly flexible and configurable post-processing pipeline can sample the dataset instances, refine and filter them, or allow domain experts to manually edit and rate them until it reaches a satisfactory quality level. This reduces manual dataset creation effort from weeks to hours, enabling data-driven RAG development early on.

We provides a command-line interface. It implements an end-to-end, configurable pipeline that converts raw documents into synthetic question and answers for RAG evaluation. It ingests PDF, DOCX, and Markdown, extracts text and splits it into chunks. Document parsing works with locally with Docling or using Mistral OCR inference endpoint. The preprocessing pipeline keeps information-rich chunks and removes low-quality segments. From curated chunks, it generates question-answer examples using an extensible set of generators. Outputs are deduplicated, then can be classified and scored using automated functions and/or LLM-based methods. The pipeline supports refinement steps such as rewriting (e.g. clarifying ambiguous questions) and query evolution (generating question variations to test robustness). A lightweight yet customizable evaluation user interface supports expert review and captures direct feedback. The workflow is driven by a single YAML configuration, so teams can parametrize sources, models, thresholds, and evaluation settings without changing code. Large language model inference can run fully locally with Ollama or via managed inference endpoints such as Open- Router or the Mistral API.

This use case targets fundamental RAG capabilities, with query types that are common across most RAG-based assistants. These include factual retrieval queries, confirmation queries (when the expected answer is yes or no), list-seeking queries that require bullet-list responses, and explanation-seeking queries that must be explicitly grounded in the source text. Complex multi-hop reasoning and hypothetical questions are out of scope in this first version because the primary aim is to evaluate the foundations of a RAG system before attempting more sophisticated queries, which are more difficult to automate and more use-case-specific. Our philosophy was to cover fewer features than other similar libraries like YourBench but to cover them with the higher quality that a technical environment like the European Space Operations Centre demands.

The benefits for AI teams are numerous. First, they obtain an initial evaluation dataset shortly after kickoff, once documents are available, rather than months later: in our case under one week, roughly a tenth of the time required by comparable projects. Second, they can measure progress per sprint and make data-driven design choices. Third, the dataset separates retriever quality from generator quality, rather than relying on end-to-end spot checks alone. Fourth, it reduces manual, error-prone test case creation in CSV and spreadsheets: generation took 24 to 32 hours, about a tenth of the effort of comparable projects, and led to a dataset roughly ten times larger. Combined, this is close to two orders of magnitude gain in productivity, leaving more effort for the core AI system. ESA Expert evaluated 96% of a random 51-item sample as clear, and correct, despite residual naturalness and realism limitations in the wording.

Spaceborne telemetry and payload measurements form multivariate time series that are inherently incomplete due to visibility gaps, transmission losses, duty cycling, and sensor anomalies. Missing data are therefore a structural characteristic of operational space systems rather than an occasional data-quality issue [1]. In addition, different subsystems are often sampled at heterogeneous frequencies, producing irregularly spaced sequences that challenge standard machine-learning models designed for uniformly sampled data [2, 3].

blocks.html: Gap-filling procedures are commonly applied to regularize these data before analysis, using methods ranging from interpolation and statistical smoothing to learning-based approaches that infer temporal dynamics from incomplete observations [4]. These techniques are typically assessed using reconstruction error alone, implicitly assuming that accurate value recovery guarantees equivalent downstream performance.

In this use case, we evaluate gap filling from a task-aware perspective by analyzing its impact on time-series forecasting. Using satellite-like telemetry with controlled missingness patterns and mixed sampling rates, we compare imputation strategies not only in terms of reconstruction quality but also in their effect on predictive accuracy and temporal consistency.

To quantify how gap-filling affects downstream intelligence rather than reconstruction alone, we design two controlled experiments on a synthetic multivariate time series mimicking typical spacecraft telemetry dynamics.

We generate a four-channel time series combining periodic, trend, and nonlinear components. Let i = 1, . . . , N, then the four channels are defined as: x1,i = sin (2πMi/N), x2,i = cos (2πMi/n),x3i = 5i/N and N(0, σ2) is added to each channel. In what follows N = 20000, M = 150, σ2 = 0.2. The first half of the sequence contains randomly injected missing values (20%), while the second half remains complete and is used for evaluation. This setup reproduces degraded historical telemetry with reliable recent observations.

We compare three learning-based imputation approaches: SAITS [5], a self-attention-based architecture for multivariate time-series imputation, implemented using the PyPOTS library [6]; TSPulse, a pulse-driven temporal representation model for sparse sequence reconstruction; Chronos2, a foundation time-series model adapted here for masked imputation [7]. All the models have been trained on window of 512 values. Linear interpolation is used as a classical baseline. The test data has been polluted with different percentage of missing values [10%,20%,30%,40%,50%] and different maximum length of consecutive gaps [20,50,100,200]. For each model, we compute the average relative reconstruction error with respect to linear interpolation Erec aging all the pollution schema, and the results are displayed in Table 2. blocks.html: To assess operational consequences, we train a forecasting model using the dsipts library [8] with an iTransformer architecture [9], using a context window of 256 and prediction horizon of 128. The test set has been equally split in two: the first part has been used for training and validating the forecasting model, the last part has been used as final test set. The model is trained under five data conditions: Full data (oracle reference), Incomplete data without imputation (half of the full data), and four interpolated training set (Linear, SAITS, TSPulse, Chronos2). The train dataset has been polluted with 50% of missing data and imputed with the filling models aforementioned.
Forecasting performance is measured through the relative forecasting error normalized by the oracle experiment Efor
rel = RMSEmodel/RMSEfull-data, and the results, averaged on all the future horizons, are displayed in Table 3.

We observe that all the proposed methods outperform linear interpolation in the gap-filling task, as indicated by a relative reconstruction error lower than one (Table 2). Among them, SAITS achieves the best reconstruction accuracy, followed by TSPulse and Chronos.

blocks.html: When evaluating the downstream forecasting task, the superiority of SAITS is confirmed, yielding performance even better than training on a reduced subset of clean data. In contrast, TSPulse shows worse forecasting performance than Chronos, reversing the ranking observed in the reconstruction experiment.

A similar trend emerges from the per-channel analysis: lower reconstruction error during gap filling does not necessarily translate into improved forecasting accuracy. This highlights that imputation quality measured in isolation is not always predictive of downstream model performance.

Deep-learning-based data generation is increasingly adopted in time-series analysis to address practical limitations such as data scarcity, class imbalance, and restricted data access due to confidentiality constraints. By learning the underlying data distribution, generative models can produce realistic synthetic sequences that enable dataset augmentation, support privacy-preserving data sharing through anonymization, and improve model robustness when real observations are limited or incomplete [10–12].

In this use case, we train two synthetic data generators based on DiffusionTS [13] and TransFusion [14]. A subset of the real GOCE telemetry dataset, consisting of approximately 150k timestamps and 17 channels, is used to train the generative model with a window size of 384 (1 encoder layer, 8 decoder layers, 4 attention heads, hidden dimension

96) for 25k epochs. The generated samples are then used as a surrogate training dataset for the same downstream predictive pipeline adopted in the previous experiments (context window 64, prediction horizon 32, trained for 100 epochs). Two different strategies of enriching has been adopted: substitution and augmentation. Starting from the initial training dataset of ∼95k real samples, in the first we replace some percentage of original samples with synthetic data, in the latter we enlarge the number of samples by a given percentage. The forecasting error is evaluated on a test set of ∼40k time points, temporally consecutive to those used for training both the generator and the forecasting models. The RMSE is computed per forecasting lag and per parameter, and the distribution of the errors is reported in Table 4 (a selected subset of lags and percentage of synthetic data used is reported for brevity).

blocks.html: We observe that using a smaller but representative synthetic training dataset can yield performance comparable to, and in some cases better than, training on only real data, expecially for large lags. These findings suggest that a compact set of representative synthetic samples may effectively guide the learning process of downstream forecasting models.

The two generation processes has been used for create synthetic data related to the OPS-SAT anomaly detection dataset [15] where both supervised and unsupervised models has been compared. Following the benchmark solution outlined in [16], statistical and structural features were extracted from each segment, including the mean, variance, total number of peaks, and the variance of the inter-peak intervals. These features were calculated across both nominal and anomalous segments for both empirical and generated samples. The performance is reported using the Matthews Correlation Coefficient [17] (MCC) computed as median value over 20 simulations with different seeds and reported in Table 5.

blocks.title: Synthetic images for Space debris classification

blocks.html: Managing the growing population of uncontrolled objects in Earth orbit has become a central concern for space agencies and satellite operators alike. Ground-based optical survey systems play a critical role in cataloging space debris, but automated detection pipelines continue to struggle with high false positive rates and poor sensitivity to faint, fast-moving objects. Current streak detection tools such as StreakDet [18] were not designed with modern machine learning classifiers in mind, and the training data required to improve these classifiers is difficult to obtain at scale.

Training a reliable classifier for space debris detection requires examples that span the full range of observational difficulty — from bright, clearly resolved streaks to faint detections at the noise floor (SNR 2.5–4). The real dataset is naturally biased toward easier cases, leaving classifiers under-trained on precisely the scenarios where automated detection is most needed and most prone to failure.

Collecting more labeled real data is slow, costly, and constrained by telescope time. Manual labeling is laborintensive and subject to expert availability. Moreover, real observations cannot be controlled — rare geometries, specific SNR levels, or particular artifact combinations cannot be generated on demand. This work investigates whether synthetic FITS images, generated to match the photometric and geometric characteristics of STREET dataset [18], can serve as a viable substitute or supplement for real labeled examples in training debris classifiers. The objective is to develop a generation pipeline grounded in the statistical properties of real observations. The pipeline is calibrated against over 50,000 ML-validated detections and produces images indistinguishable from real data at the feature level, without requiring additional observational resources.

The proposed pipeline is structured in three broad phases. The first is calibration: statistical distributions of key observational parameters — streak length, angle, SNR, elongation, background level, and artifact occurrence rates — are extracted from over 50,000 real detections in the STREET archive. These distributions serve as the generative prior, ensuring synthetic outputs are grounded in the empirical properties of real data rather than arbitrary assumptions.

The second phase is generation: synthetic scenes are constructed by placing a star field alongside a streak source with randomised geometry and intensity. Each scene is rendered through a physics-based pipeline that applies optical diffraction via a Point Spread Function, structured sky background and sensor noise, and CCD bloom artefacts. The parameters governing these effects, namely, background levels, noise characteristics, flux distributions are calibrated against the statistical distributions extracted from real STREET observations in the preceding phase, ensuring that synthetic outputs reflect the true diversity of conditions encountered across the STREET Dataset’s sensor network. An example of generated image can be seen in Figure 2.

blocks.caption: Example of generated image with faint streak, stars and saturation blooms.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: The third phase is validation: the synthetic dataset is evaluated both statistically, using Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests and Wasserstein distance to confirm distributional alignment with real data, and functionally, by measuring whether an MLP classifier [19] trained on mixed real and synthetic data outperforms one trained on real data alone, particularly on low-SNR examples where the data scarcity problem is most acute. Ground truth labels are drawn from the ML-validated STREET detection catalogue, while StreakDet is used as a fixed feature extractor, ensuring that synthetic fidelity is assessed against the same pipeline applied to real observations. This approach offers a reproducible template for addressing data scarcity in other astronomical survey contexts where labeled examples are expensive, rare, or impossible to collect on demand.
The SYNDAQ results demonstrate that realistic synthetic data can be generated across modalities (text, time series, images).

The observed benefits include significant time savings (e.g., reducing RAG evaluation dataset creation from weeks to hours), improved exploration of edge cases (rare geometries, specific artifacts), and guaranteed label correctness. While synthetic data can match real data in downstream tasks, reconstruction quality alone is not a reliable proxy for (e.g., forecasting) performance.
